meta.headline: Does a heat pump always cost less to run than oil, propane or baseboard heat?
meta.seoTitle: Heat pump vs oil, propane and baseboard running costs

dek.text: Against propane and electric resistance heat, the studies here find a heat pump cheaper to run in almost every case; against oil, which heat is cheaper depends on the price of oil and on how cold it is outside.

assertions.text: Compared against electrical resistance and propane heating, mini-splits proved more cost-effective for all energy prices and outdoor temperatures; for oil-fired systems, the relative energy price determines the temperature above which a mini-split became more cost-effective.
qualifications: "The studies here find" and "almost every case", not a settled rule; the answer section states what the evidence cannot settle.

description.text: Studies find heat pumps cheaper to run than propane or baseboard heat almost everywhere; against oil it turns on the oil price and the outdoor temperature.

assertions.text: Compared against electrical resistance and propane heating, mini-splits proved more cost-effective for all energy prices and outdoor temperatures; for oil-fired systems, the relative energy price determines the temperature above which a mini-split became more cost-effective.
qualifications: "Studies find" and "almost everywhere", with the oil exception in the same sentence.

sections.name: hook
sections.heading: Oil, propane and baseboards: is a heat pump a sure win?

sentences.text: Most heat pump arguments are about gas, but homes that burn heating oil or propane, or run electric baseboards, are usually told that for them a heat pump is the easy win.
This article checks that promise fuel by fuel, against what studies modelled and what they measured in real homes.

sections.name: setup
sections.heading: Who says a heat pump always wins, and who disagrees

sentences.text: EnergySage, a marketplace that connects homeowners with installers, states it most broadly: "Heat pumps consistently save against propane, oil, and electric resistance heating almost everywhere."

assertions.text: EnergySage wrote that heat pumps consistently save against propane, oil and electric resistance heating almost everywhere.

quote.text: Heat pumps consistently save against propane, oil, and electric resistance heating almost everywhere.
quote.speaker: EnergySage

sentences.text: Efficiency Maine's homeowner FAQ is a little more careful, saying "heating with heat pumps is usually less expensive than heating with oil, kerosene, or propane".

assertions.text: Efficiency Maine said heating with heat pumps is usually less expensive than heating with oil, kerosene or propane.

quote.text: heating with heat pumps is usually less expensive than heating with oil, kerosene, or propane
quote.speaker: Efficiency Maine

sentences.text: Rewiring America ranks the fuels, writing that "the biggest savings will come if you switch from fuel oil, propane, or electricity as your main source of heat".

assertions.text: Rewiring America wrote that the biggest savings come from switching away from fuel oil, propane or electricity as the main source of heat.

quote.text: the biggest savings will come if you switch from fuel oil, propane, or electricity as your main source of heat
quote.speaker: Rewiring America

sentences.text: The Boston Globe reported the other side: in a winter when oil was cheaper, even Massachusetts homeowners leaving oil "could see their energy costs increase by a few hundred dollars over the cold season".

assertions.text: The Boston Globe reported that with oil cheaper that year, even Massachusetts homeowners switching from oil could see energy costs rise by a few hundred dollars over the cold season.

quote.text: could see their energy costs increase by a few hundred dollars over the cold season
quote.speaker: The Boston Globe

sections.name: investigation
sections.heading: What the studies found, fuel by fuel

sentences.text: The widest view comes from a national model by researchers at NREL and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory: of the homes heating mainly with electricity, fuel oil or propane that already have air conditioning, it estimates that 95 to 100 percent would pay less with a heat pump, at a median saving of $300 to $650 a year depending on the unit's efficiency.

assertions.text: For the homes heating primarily with electricity, fuel oil or propane and with central or room AC, 95% to 100% nationally have positive bill savings, with median savings of $300 to $650 per year depending on efficiency.
qualifications: The sentence says "estimates" and limits the result to homes that already have air conditioning; s08 gives the weaker result without it.

sentences.text: Air conditioning matters because the model has the heat pump cool the house too: for the 6 million homes on those fuels without it, only 73 to 86 percent come out ahead, and most of the homes whose bills rise are in hotter climates, where the added cooling costs more than the heating saves.

assertions.text: Only 73% to 86% of the 6 million homes heating with those fuels but without central or room AC would have positive bill savings; the installed heat pumps are assumed to be used for AC in these homes.
Most of the homes with increased energy bills are in hotter climates without existing AC, where increased cooling costs outweigh heating cost savings.

sentences.text: Gas homes with air conditioning, where most heat pump advice starts, fare worse in the same model: their median runs from a $70 loss with the lowest-performing heat pump to a $380 saving with the highest.

assertions.text: For the 46 million homes heating with natural gas and with AC, median bill savings ranged from -$70 to $380 per year depending on heat pump performance level.
qualifications: Like for like with s07: both groups have air conditioning, both are medians that vary with the heat pump's performance.

sentences.text: A model is an estimate, so the next question is what heat pumps did in homes where they were measured.

A field assessment of cold-climate heat pumps found that the all-electric systems cut heating costs by 53 percent on average, measured against a baseline that assumed an electric resistance heater would have met the same load.

assertions.text: For all-electric systems, with an electric resistance heater assumed to meet the same load in the baseline, average cost savings were 53%.
qualifications: The sentence names the assumed resistance baseline; the callout after the table says what that leaves out.

blocks.caption: Measured savings from cold-climate heat pumps in a field assessment, each row against its own baseline

rows.label: All-electric systems against an assumed electric resistance heater, average cost saving

sentences.text: Because the field assessment set its all-electric savings against an assumed electric resistance heater, its results cannot show how a heat pump does against a home that burns oil.

assertions.text: For the ductless and all-electric ducted systems, the load met by the heat pump was assumed to have been met by an electric resistance heater in the baseline case.
qualifications: This callout is the limit on s11: the baseline is resistance heat, not oil.

sentences.text: An evaluation of ductless mini-split heat pumps found them cheaper to run than electric resistance and propane heat at every energy price and every outdoor temperature it examined.

assertions.text: Compared against electrical resistance and propane heating, ductless mini-split heat pumps proved more cost-effective for all energy prices and all outdoor air temperatures.
qualifications: s14 gives the same study's exception for oil straight after.

sentences.text: Oil was the exception: the price of oil relative to electricity set the outdoor temperature above which the mini-split was the cheaper heat.

assertions.text: For oil-fired systems, the relative energy price determines the temperature above which a mini-split became more cost-effective.
qualifications: The callout after s14 gives the thresholds and their dependence on price.

sentences.text: The evaluators advised oil-heated homes to switch the mini-split off in very cold weather, when the oil system would run cheaper: below 8 degrees Fahrenheit in 2015 and below 25 degrees in 2016, depending on energy prices and on how the units performed in the cold.

assertions.text: Oil-heated homeowners should turn off the mini-split in very cold conditions, below 8F in 2015 and below 25F in 2016, when an oil-fired system would operate less expensively, depending on energy prices and cold-temperature COPs.
qualifications: Each threshold is tied to its year; the sentence says they depend on prices and cold-weather performance.

sentences.text: They added that if oil prices rise against electricity rates, that switchover temperature may move lower, allowing the heat pump to run all winter.

assertions.text: If oil prices increase against electric energy rates, the switchover temperature from oil to mini-split heat may move lower, allowing continual use of the mini-split.

sentences.text: Another study found the same ordering by fuel: where homes heat with electricity or fuels other than gas, heating is generally more expensive and the net benefits of a heat pump are higher, though climate and energy prices also play an important role.

assertions.text: In regions where the heating source is electricity or fuels other than natural gas, heating is generally more expensive and the net benefits of heat pumps are higher; climate and energy prices also play an important role.
qualifications: The sentence keeps the study's own caveat about climate and energy prices.

sentences.text: Data from 273 completed electrification retrofits point the same way: the large cuts in annual energy cost were most likely in homes that had high bills beforehand, such as those heating with propane or fuel oil, while some projects raised costs, by as much as $1,000 a year in some cases.

assertions.text: Among 273 electrification projects with cost savings data, high reductions in annual energy cost were most likely in homes with high pre-retrofit bills, such as those heating with propane or fuel oil, while some projects increased post-retrofit energy costs, by as much as $1,000 per year in some cases.
qualifications: The sentence says "electrification retrofits", not heat pumps alone, and "most likely", the passage's own modality.

blocks.caption: Home electrification projects with cost data: how many there were and the largest yearly cost increase among them.

sentences.text: Counting what the equipment costs as well as the fuel, RMI found that in parts of New England without gas, heat pumps have a lower net present cost than both oil- and propane-fired systems, and recommends prioritising oil and propane customers, for whom it finds the greatest immediate cost benefit.

assertions.text: In New England areas that lack gas infrastructure and rely on heating oil or propane, heat pumps have a lower net present cost than both heating oil- and propane-fired systems.
qualifications: "Net present cost" names the measure; the callout after it gives the study that found otherwise for oil.

assertions.text: RMI recommends prioritising electrification for customers using heating oil or propane, as it has the greatest immediate carbon and cost benefit for them.

sentences.text: A study of the private economics of US home heat pumps, counting the cost of buying the heat pump over its life as well as the fuel, reached a different result for oil: switching usually leaves an oil-heated homeowner worse off, and nearly 65 percent of oil-heated houses are in cold climates, while replacing resistance heat almost always produces a clear benefit and replacing propane is often economical.

assertions.text: Heat pump adoption in fuel oil heated homes usually causes the homeowner a private economic loss, and nearly 65% of fuel oil heated houses are in cold climates; switching from electric resistance almost always produces a clear benefit, and replacing propane is often economical to the homeowner.
qualifications: The sentence names the measure as lifetime cost, equipment as well as fuel, so it reads as the counterpart of s19 and not as a running-cost result.

sentences.text: A British study of heat pump customers fits the resistance-heat case: electricity use rose least after installation, and in fact fell, for those who had heated with electricity before; but it measures electricity use rather than bills, and the great majority of its customers had a gas boiler before, so it cannot speak to oil or propane.

assertions.text: The increase in electricity consumption after installing a heat pump was lowest, indeed negative, for customers who previously had electric heating; the great majority of customers in the sample had a gas boiler previously.
qualifications: The sentence says what the study measured and whom it sampled.

sentences.text: A Canadian policy report, citing Natural Resources Canada, puts the energy saving against baseboards at up to 65 percent and infers from that figure significant savings on the power bill for those switching from baseboards; the bill saving is the report's inference, not a measurement, and it compares heat pumps with baseboards only.

assertions.text: Heat pumps use up to 65 per cent less energy than standard electric resistance heating (baseboards), meaning anyone switching from baseboard heating will see significant cost savings on their power bill.
qualifications: The sentence keeps "up to", marks the bill saving as the report's inference from an energy figure, and limits the comparison to baseboards.

sections.name: answer
sections.heading: So does a heat pump always cost less to run?

sentences.text: Against propane and electric resistance heat, this evidence says nearly always: the mini-split evaluation found it cheaper at every price and temperature it examined, and the national model found lower bills for almost all such homes that already had air conditioning.

assertions.text: Compared against electrical resistance and propane heating, mini-splits proved more cost-effective for all energy prices and outdoor temperatures; almost all electricity-, oil- or propane-heated homes with AC have positive bill savings.
qualifications: "Nearly always", and the model result is limited to homes with air conditioning.

sentences.text: Against oil, not always: the heat pump wins above a switchover temperature that moves with the price of oil, and the studies that count equipment cost disagree on whether leaving oil pays.

assertions.text: For oil-fired systems, the relative energy price determines the temperature above which a mini-split is more cost-effective.
Counting the homeowner's private economics, heat pump adoption in fuel oil heated homes usually causes a private economic loss.
qualifications: Stated as a disagreement with s19, not as the answer.

sentences.text: Why the studies split on oil is not something this evidence settles: they range from national models to measured homes and lifetime-cost estimates, and the mini-split evaluation found that cost-effectiveness depends on the heating system being replaced, the energy prices of the period and the outdoor temperature.

assertions.text: The cost-effectiveness of mini-splits used for heating depends on alternative heating systems, energy prices for a given period, and outside air temperatures.
qualifications: This callout says the split is not explained, only what one study says drives it.

sentences.text: Nor can it price a particular house: the results moved with whether the home already had air conditioning, with climate and with energy prices.

assertions.text: Fewer oil-, propane- and electricity-heated homes without AC had positive bill savings, and climate and energy prices play an important role in heat pump net benefits.

sections.name: takeaway
sections.heading: What to check before you switch

sentences.text: If you heat with propane or baseboards, the open question is less whether a heat pump will run cheaper than what it will cost to install, so set installed quotes against what you spend on fuel each winter.
If you heat with oil, ask an installer below what outdoor temperature your old system becomes the cheaper heat at this winter's prices, and whether you will keep it for those days.
And if you have no air conditioning now, remember that a heat pump brings cooling with it, and cooling adds to the bill.
